clinicalPearls: A rare bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that follows penetrating ocular trauma or intraocular surgery to one eye
The injured eye is termed the exciting eye and the fellow, initially uninjured eye that becomes inflamed is the sympathising eye
Onset is usually within weeks to months of the inciting injury, though it can occur many years later
Classic fundus findings include Dalen-Fuchs nodules (yellow-white deposits at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium) and a diffuse choroiditis
Presentation may include bilateral blurred vision, photophobia, pain and, in some cases, features overlapping with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease
Management principles rely on prompt, high-intensity systemic corticosteroids followed by steroid-sparing systemic immunosuppression to preserve the sympathising eye
Early enucleation of a blind, severely injured exciting eye may be considered to prevent onset, but once inflammation begins its benefit is uncertain
Lifelong monitoring is needed because the disease is chronic and prone to recurrent flares
reference.pathophysiology: Sympathetic ophthalmia is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune granulomatous inflammation directed against previously sequestered uveal and retinal antigens. Penetrating trauma or surgery exposes these ocular antigens to the systemic immune system, breaking immune privilege and sensitising the host. The resulting autoreactive response attacks the uvea of both eyes, producing a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis characterised by diffuse choroidal infiltration by lymphocytes and epithelioid cells and by Dalen-Fuchs nodules. Because the response targets shared antigens, the uninjured sympathising eye is affected in parallel with the exciting eye.
additionalInvestigations: Fundus fluorescein angiography showing multiple early hyperfluorescent leakage points and late pooling
Indocyanine green angiography demonstrating hypofluorescent choroidal lesions
Optical coherence tomography to detect subretinal fluid and choroidal thickening
Fundus autofluorescence to map Dalen-Fuchs nodules and outer retinal changes
Ultrasonography where media are opaque, to assess choroidal thickening
Systemic and infective screening (including tuberculosis, syphilis and sarcoidosis) to exclude mimics
redFlags: Any new inflammation in the fellow eye after penetrating trauma or surgery, which is sympathetic ophthalmia until proven otherwise
Rapidly progressive bilateral visual loss requiring urgent immunosuppression
Exudative retinal detachment threatening the macula
Development of the disease in a patient's only functioning eye
reference.prognosis: With prompt and sustained immunosuppression, many patients retain useful vision, but the disease is chronic and relapsing; delayed treatment or recurrent flares can lead to severe bilateral visual loss and secondary complications such as cataract, glaucoma and macular scarring.
pitfalls: Attributing fellow-eye inflammation to something benign and missing early sympathetic ophthalmia
Under-dosing or prematurely tapering immunosuppression and precipitating a relapse
Assuming enucleation of the exciting eye after onset will halt established disease
Failing to exclude infective and neoplastic mimics before committing to long-term immunosuppression
Overlooking the risk following seemingly minor intraocular surgery, not just major trauma
management: Institute prompt high-intensity systemic corticosteroids to control the bilateral granulomatous panuveitis and preserve the sympathising eye
Add steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as mycophenolate, azathioprine, methotrexate or ciclosporin, with TNF-inhibitor biologics for refractory disease
Use topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics as adjuncts for anterior segment inflammation
Consider enucleation of a blind, painful exciting eye, while exhausting the visual potential before removing any seeing eye
Exclude infective mimics such as tuberculosis, syphilis and sarcoidosis before and during immunosuppression
Monitor for and manage complications including cataract, glaucoma and macular scarring, and screen for immunosuppressant toxicity
Manage under an ophthalmology and uveitis specialist with long-term surveillance for relapse
